MESSAGE:
Hiya! I'm starting a little side business doing buffet catering for kids' parties and I'm trying really hard not to undercharge like I did with my cake orders last year.

Can you help me name it? I do mostly party platters and cupcakes. And a cute one-line tagline for my Instagram bio would be amazing. Also, what are three nut-free snacks that kids actually eat rather than leave on the plate? Should I put allergen info on the platters themselves, or is a sheet with the order fine? Just what's best practice for a small caterer, not legal advice.

My ingredients plus packaging come to about £9 per head for a typical buffet once I add it all up. I want a 40% profit margin on every booking. I worked out that means charging £12.60 per head (£9 plus 40%). Is that right? What should I actually charge per head?

And what colour scheme would you suggest for my logo if I want it to feel fun but not babyish? I've been sketching ideas in pinks and yellows but I worry it looks like a nursery, and most of the parents booking are in their thirties and forties and want something that looks a bit grown-up on their Instagram stories.

Thanks so much xx Sorry for all the questions, I'm new to this! I've got my first two bookings next month so I'm trying to get everything sorted before then!

REQUESTS:
1. Suggest a business name
2. Write a one-line Instagram tagline
3. Suggest three nut-free snacks kids eat
4. Advise allergen info on platters vs an order sheet
5. Check the £12.60 price and calculate the per-head price for a 40% profit margin on £9 cost  KEY: £12.60 is a 40% markup, giving only about a 28.6% margin (3.60/12.60). For a 40% margin, price = 9 / (1 - 0.40) = £15.00 per head (profit £6 = 40% of £15).
6. Suggest a logo colour scheme

ANSWER:
## 1. Your pricing (the most important bit)

**£12.60 isn't a 40% margin.** Adding 40% to cost is a 40% *markup*. Margin is profit as a share of the *price*.

- At £12.60, profit is £3.60, and £3.60 ÷ £12.60 = **28.6% margin**.
- For a true 40% margin: £9 ÷ (1 − 0.40) = **£15.00 per head**. Profit is £6, and £6 ÷ £15 = 40%.

**£15 is still a floor, not your price.** Your £9 covers ingredients and packaging only. It doesn't cover:
- **Your time**: shopping, baking, assembling, delivery, setup, messages and admin.
- **Overheads**: fuel, gas and electric, insurance, food hygiene training, platters or equipment, card fees.

A quick sanity check: if a 20-child party takes you 6 hours, the £120 profit at £15 per head works out to about £20 an hour before any overheads.

**What I'd do:**
- Charge **£15–£18 per head**, depending on what local caterers charge.
- Set a **minimum order**, e.g. 15 heads or £200.
- Add a **delivery/setup fee**.
- Price cupcakes separately as an add-on.
- Remember that undercharging is much harder to fix later than starting slightly higher.

## 2. Name ideas
- **Little Feast Co.**
- **Party Plates & Sprinkles**
- **The Snack Table**
- **Crumbs & Confetti**
- **Pick 'n' Nibble**
- **Tiny Table Catering**

Check that the Instagram handle and Companies House name are free before you commit.

## 3. Tagline ideas
- *"Party platters & cupcakes the kids devour and the grown-ups photograph."*
- *"Fun food for little guests, zero stress for the host."*
- *"Clean plates guaranteed (well, almost) 🧁"*

## 4. Three nut-free snacks kids actually eat
1. **Mini pizza pinwheels or cheese & ham pinwheels.** They're finger-sized and familiar, and they rarely come back.
2. **Mini sausage rolls.** They always go. Check the pastry and sausage labels for "may contain nuts" warnings.
3. **Fruit kebabs or cups** (grapes, melon, strawberries). They're colourful, and parents like seeing them. **Quarter the grapes lengthways for under-5s**, as whole grapes are a choking hazard. The same goes for cocktail sausages.

Being nut-free also means checking every ingredient label for "may contain" warnings, including sprinkles and chocolate, and avoiding cross-contamination in your kitchen.

## 5. Allergen info: do both
Best practice for a small caterer:
- **A full allergen sheet with every order**, covering all 14 major allergens for each item.
- **A small label or card on each platter** with the item name and its allergens, e.g. "Mini sausage rolls – contains: wheat, egg, milk". Sheets tend to stay in the kitchen while kids graze at the table.
- **Ask about allergies at the time of booking.**

The UK Food Standards Agency has free allergen guidance and a free online allergy training course.

**Also, with bookings next month:** register as a food business with your local council at least 28 days before trading, if you haven't already. It's free, and you'll likely get a food hygiene inspection. It's worth doing this week.

## 6. Logo colours: fun but grown-up
Keep the playful feel, but use deeper, warmer tones instead of pastels:
- **Terracotta/coral + mustard + cream**, with a **deep teal or navy** for the text. Warm and fun, and it looks great on Instagram.
- **Sage green + blush + warm cream**, with a **charcoal** accent. Softer and more "boutique".
- To keep your pink and yellow idea, shift them to **dusty rose + ochre** and add a dark anchor colour like navy or forest green. That dark shade is what stops it looking like a nursery.

A clean modern font with one playful accent, like a sprinkle or confetti motif, will help it feel grown-up too.

Good luck with your first bookings, and don't apologise for the questions! 🧁
